Similarly, biochar, commonly applied in environmental protection such as soil remediation, has a rougher pore structure and lower specific surface area. In contrast, mesoporous carbon, with its larger surface area and adjustable pore configuration, demonstrates superior performance in advanced applications like energy storage, catalysis, gas separation, and biomedicine (Zhang et al., 2024; Mehdipour-Ataei and Aram, 2023; Yuan et al., 2022). Mesoporous carbon materials with various pore sizes and pore structures can be synthesized via different methods. Their unique properties have made them a suitable choice for various applications, such as energy-storage batteries, supercapacitors, biosensors, fuel cells, adsorption/separation of various molecules, catalysts/catalyst support, enzyme immobilization, and drug delivery, in different fields. This review covers the fabrication techniques of mesoporous carbon structures and their typical applications in various fields and features a brief introduction of the functionalization and modification of mesoporous carbons. 1. Introduction Porous carbon materials have been a focus of attention in chemistry, physics, and material sciences in recent decades because of their unique structures, physiochemical properties, superior chemical/mechanical stability, good electrical conductivity, and low cost. Generally, different carbon-based structures, including carbon nanotubes, fullerenes, porous carbons, have been widely applied for various applications, such as adsorbents for the purification of water [1,2]. Among them, porous carbons are attractive because their synthesis methods are very simple and the properties of these materials are much better than other carbon-based materials thanks to their porous structure. On the other hand, the well-porous structures support the incorporation of new functional agents such as organic or inorganic components within the porous channels or on the surface of the carbon walls, which significantly improve their properties and performance in various applications. Porous carbon materials have been applied for many years in various applications, including energy storage and conversion, gas separation, water purification, catalysis, and sensing [3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10]. According to the definition of the international federation of pure and applied chemistry (IUPAC), porous carbon materials can be divided into three groups according to pore size: microporous carbon (materials with pore diameter less than 2 nm), mesoporous carbon (materials with pore diameter between 2 and 50 nm), and macroporous carbon (materials with pore diameter larger than 50 nm) [11]. Among them, mesoporous carbon structures with a broad or narrow distribution of pores have recently attracted enormous attention in different fields because of high specific surface area, good chemical and mechanical properties, high thermal stability, large pore volume, and uniform and controllable porous structure. These outstanding properties enable mesoporous structures to be excellent candidates for various practical applications, including as a catalyst and its support, adsorption and separation, energy conversion and storage, environmental remediation, drug delivery, and biomedical applications [12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19]. At first, mesopores in carbon structures were produced by enlarging micropores via oxidation during activation process, such as activated carbons, or at the interstices between carbon particles, such as carbon aerogels. The first technique led to a significant reduction in the yield of carbon, and the second one’s morphology was difficult to control. Thus, new methods have been developed for producing of mesoporous carbons [20]. In this regard, the first study on the synthesis of mesoporous carbon materials was reported in 1999 by Ryoo et al. [21]. They used mesoporous silica as a hard template and sucrose as a carbon source to produce a mesoporous structure with high specific surface areas and tunable pore diameters between 2 and 50 nm. This invention has attracted much attention from many researchers for the preparation and potential application of mesoporous carbon materials. Rapid progress has been made in the field of mesoporous carbon material synthesis using the self-assembly of copolymer molecular arrays and carbon precursors, by Dai and Zhao’ groups [22,23]. Different templates with various structures can be used for the preparation of mesoporous materials with a high level of control over their structures. For example, several mesoporous silica materials with various structures, such as SBA-1, SBA-15, SBA-16, MCM-48, KIT-6, and KIT-5, are applied as templates for the synthesis of mesoporous carbon materials with different mesoporous structures [24,25,26]. The production of mesoporous carbons through hard mesoporous silica templates has led to structures with surface areas of more than 2000 m2 g−1, a higher pore volume of up to 3.0 cm3 g−1, and tunable pore diameters, along with high conductivity. Furthermore, a similar hard-templating method was also used by Hyeon et al. for the fabrication of ordered porous carbon using phenolic resin as the source of carbon [27,28]. Numerous approaches are used to synthesize mesoporous carbon materials, including (a) activation methods (physical activation and chemical activation), (b) template methods (hard template and soft template), (c) carbonized method (the carbonization of polymer/polymer blends, organic aerogels, etc.), and (d) catalytic activation using metal ions. fetched_contents.text: Insight into activated carbon from different kinds of chemical activating agents: A review Introduction Activated carbon (AC), also called activated charcoal, is basically defined as black carbonaceous porous solid material with high specific surface area, reasonable pore size distribution and high-degree of surface reactivity (Brito et al., 2018; Sayğılı and Sayğılı, 2019; Yahya et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018). AC is amorphous and non-graphitic microcrystalline with a turbostratic structure (Xia and Shi, 2016). The size and thickness of each microcrystal is approximately 1–3 nm and 1–1.3 nm, respectively. The synthesis of AC consists of two basic procedures: carbonization and activation (Ayinla et al., 2019; Kleszyk et al., 2015). The purpose of carbonization is to reduce the volatile content of raw materials via pyrolysis of the carbon precursors in the temperature range of 300–900 °C and to create char with primary porosity associated with a high content of fixed carbon. The purpose of activation is to improve the specific surface area or pore volume of AC through opening new pores and developing the existing pores. Apart from that, activation can vary or adjust the surface chemical nature of AC with certain unique characteristics. Activation is considered to be more crucial than carbonization in terms of the properties of AC. Hence, more attention has been paid to its activation. Presently, three main activation techniques are used to produce AC: physical activation, chemical activation, and physio-chemical activation (Arslanoğlu, 2019; Fu et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2016; Oginni et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2019a). Physical activation is a dual-stage process, that features the carbonization stage in the presence of an inert gas (N2 or Ar) followed by the activation stage with the aid of an oxidizing gas (O2, CO2, H2O steam) in the temperature range of 800–1200 °C (Balahmar et al., 2017; Danish and Ahmad, 2018; Yin et al., 2014). The most important benefits of physical activation are its clean, green production without any secondary waste disposals compared to chemical activation. Nevertheless, the disadvantages of physical activation are related to its high activation temperature, considerably long processing time, relatively low carbon yield, and poor specific surface area. The main factors affecting physical activation include the type of carbon precursors, their particle size, gas flow, heating rate, carbonization time, and carbonization temperature. Chemical activation, known as “wet oxidation,” is a single-stage process, during which carbonization and activation take place simultaneously in the temperature range of 450–850 °C (González-García, 2018; Kılıç et al., 2012). The advantages of chemical activation are its low heating temperature, short processing time, high carbon yield, well-controlled porosity, and high specific surface area (Nayak et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014; Zhang and Shen, 2019). However, the disadvantages of chemical activation include its drastic corrosivity and inevitable washing process (Chen et al., 2012; Dai et al., 2018). The main factors affecting chemical activation include the type of activating agent, mixing method, mass ratio of activating agent to carbon precursor, and heating method (Sevilla and Mokaya, 2014). Physio-chemical activation is a combination of physical and chemical processes, involving the chemical impregnation of carbon precursors with activating agents, followed by a physical activation step under an oxidizing gas atmosphere. The advantages of physio-chemical activation are its controllable textural property and surface modification. The intrinsic drawbacks of physio-chemical activation are its complex and excessive energy consumption, which restrict its large-scale application within industry. Of these techniques, chemical activation is considered to be the most promising method for the production of AC with excellent performance. Furthermore, the activating agents play decisive roles in the formation of pores or surface chemical groups during the activation. In terms of application, AC has been extensively used in water purification, energy storage, and as a catalyst with the rapid development of social economic (Elmouwahidi et al., 2017; Karadirek and Okkay, 2018; Kumar and Jena, 2016; Li et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020a, Zhang et al., 2020b). Due to the importance of AC in many fields, a high volume of studies, including research papers, short communications and reviews, have been reported. In a study by Yahya et al., the preparation of AC derived from agricultural residues was presented (Yahya et al., 2015). A review done by Jain et al. reported new findings about enhancing the porosity of AC via the hydrothermal treatment of biomass waste before the activation process (Jain et al., 2016). González-García reviewed the synthesis, textural characterization, surface chemistry, and adsorption features of AC from lignocellulosic precursors (González-García, 2018). Rashidi et al. gave a comprehensive discussion, which was focused on the influences of different heating methods on the obtained AC (Rashidi and Yusup, 2017). Sevilla and Mokaya presented a method for tailoring the porosity and morphology of biomass-based AC for their application in supercapacitors and hydrogen storage (Sevilla and Mokaya, 2014). Bi et al. summarized the carbon materials with different geometrical dimensions derived from biomasses with various biological structures (Bi et al., 2019). However, from the literature, it is determined that the targeted review on AC activating agents still remains poorly documented. Therefore, this study pays special attention to scientific information regarding the pore-forming mechanisms, the influences of various activating agents on the synthesis procedure, and the physio-chemical characteristics of AC. fetched_contents.text: Mesoporous Carbon: A Versatile Material for Scientific Applications Abstract Mesoporous carbon is a promising material having multiple applications. It can act as a catalytic support and can be used in energy storage devices. Moreover, mesoporous carbon controls body’s oral drug delivery system and adsorb poisonous metal from water and various other molecules from an aqueous solution. The accuracy and improved activity of the carbon materials depend on some parameters. The recent breakthrough in the synthesis of mesoporous carbon, with high surface area, large pore-volume, and good thermostability, improves its activity manifold in performing functions. Considering the promising application of mesoporous carbon, it should be broadly illustrated in the literature. This review summarizes the potential application of mesoporous carbon in many scientific disciplines. Moreover, the outlook for further improvement of mesoporous carbon has been demonstrated in detail. Hopefully, it would act as a reference guidebook for researchers about the putative application of mesoporous carbon in multidimensional fields. Keywords: mesoporous carbon, surface modification, catalytic support, adsorbent, drug delivery, capacitor 1. Introduction According to IUPAC, the term “mesoporous carbon” refers to solid-based material, which might have either disordered or ordered networks with narrow or broad pores distribution in the range from 2 to 50 nm [1]. Historically, Ryoo et al. [2] reported the first structural composition of highly ordered mesoporous carbon material using mesoporous silica template, and later, much consideration was given to its synthetic methods and applications [3,4,5]. Therefore, rapid development was started for the synthesis of mesoporous carbon with the use of carbon precursors and self-assembly of copolymer molecular arrays [6,7,8,9]. Recently, modification, as well as the introduction of physicochemical properties on carbon, has been applied by incorporating inorganic constituents either anchored onto the mesoporous walls or decorated within the channels. Thus, the emergence of so-called modified mesoporous carbon has mostly driven the advancement of carbon-based electrodes or catalysts for its putative applications [10,11,12,13]. On the other hand, the substantial development of clean energy technology has motivated carbon-based researchers to exploit this porous material in the formation of energy storage devices [14,15,16,17,18]. Porous carbon materials, including carbon molecular sieves and activated carbon, have been synthesized on a large scale from fruit shells, wood, coal, or polymers by simple pyrolysis and physical or chemical treatment at elevated temperatures [19,20,21,22,23]. Moreover, these carbons have relatively broad pore-size distributions in both mesopore and micropore ranges and have been synthesized from defects resulting from heteroatoms elimination during carbonization. However, the carbon materials produced in these methods provide poor conductivity, structural integrity, and mass transport, owing to the presence of heteroatoms, lack of structural control, and restricted flow pathways. These limitations have been resolved by the introduction of mesopores for potential applications [24,25]. Mesoporous carbons with good physical properties are being synthesized on a large scale by carbonization from organic sources, such as sucrose, under acid treatment using silica templates. In this protocol, a transient silica-carbon complex is formed, and finally, following the alkali treatment, the silica is removed, leaving mesoporous carbon with analogous properties of silica materials (Figure 5) [24,25]. The mesoporous carbon synthesis, in this way, possesses good structural features and meets high physiological demands in modern scientific research [17,21,22,23]. Carbon materials with well-ordered mesoporous structures are ubiquitous and indispensable in modern scientific research, which attracted huge attention for their promising applications in various fields, including adsorption and separation of large biomolecules, electrical double-layer capacitors, catalytic support, wastewater treatment, and air purification (Figure 1) [26,27,28,29,30,31,32]. The emergence of inorganic porous materials, such as silica, zeolite, zeotype materials, carbon, metal oxides, and composites, has paved the way for the progression of drug delivery systems and other applications due to their high adsorption efficiency and ideal biocompatibility [33,34,35,36,37,38,39]. Compared with conventional porous materials, an inorganic carrier with small particle sizes, well-control shape, high stability, surface functionalization properties, low density, and wide availability offers substantial benefits in terms of application [40,41]. Recent advances in nanotechnology have provided a new dimension in carbon structure through continuous development of conventional methods as well as the introduction of new synthesis techniques [42]. Considering the well-controlled structure and promising application of mesoporous carbon in many scientific disciplines, it should be broadly compiled in the scientific literature from different points of view. To this line, the article aimed to provide a brief but elaborate overview of the applications of mesoporous carbon in many scientific research fields with special emphasis on catalytic reaction, adsorption, and drug delivery. Moreover, the outlook for further improvements and plausible challenges of mesoporous carbon has been demonstrated in detail. The authors, therefore, hope that this article would serve as a reference guidebook for future researchers regarding the potential application of mesoporous carbon in diverse research fields 2. Branch report on procedural differences in chemical activation

Chemical activation differs from physical activation primarily by using chemical reagents rather than only heat and gas to develop porosity. The evidence points to specific activators such as H₃PO₄, KOH, ZnCl₂, and others being used to promote bond cleavage and protect internal pore structure during activation [N1-R2][N3-R5]. In the context of mesoporous carbon, chemical activation is described as involving the thermal decomposition of a carbon precursor impregnated with suitable chemical agents, with temperatures typically in a range that is lower than physical activation [N2-R4]. The role of these chemicals is twofold: they assist in forming pores through degradation, dehydration, and complexation, while also preserving the pore structure [N4-R2][N1-R4].

Thermal conditions for chemical activation are generally lower than those for physical activation. One review source says chemical activation occurs in the temperature range of 450–850 °C, while physical activation is a dual-stage process in the range of 800–1200 °C [N6-F2]. Another source notes that chemical activation is advantageous because it operates at lower temperatures than physical activation, which is a key procedural difference [N3-R1]. The evidence also indicates that chemical activation is a single-stage process in which carbonization and activation occur simultaneously [N6-F2], whereas physical activation is more conventionally split into carbonization followed by activation [N6-F2].

Before activation, the precursor is treated with an activator. The evidence shows that precursor chemistry is central to mesoporous carbon synthesis, with carbon sources such as sucrose, phenolic resin, and other materials reacting with metal precursors or being impregnated with activators before thermal treatment [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The precursor is therefore not left in a raw state but is chemically modified before activation. In practice, this means impregnation with activators such as H₃PO₄ or other chemical agents is a standard preparatory step [N1-R2][N3-R5]. The review also emphasizes that the preparation method directly influences pore structure, specific surface area, pore volume, and surface chemistry, which in turn determines material performance [N6-F1].

Overall, chemical activation is a reagent-driven, lower-temperature, single-stage process in which the precursor is impregnated with activators to control porosity development [N1-R2][N2-R4][N6-F2]. This contrasts with the downstream physical activation branch, where the procedure is gas- and temperature-dependent rather than chemical-agent-dependent.
node_outputs.N9:
Branch report on procedural differences in physical activation

Physical activation relies on controlled burn-off gases and atmosphere conditions rather than chemical reagents. The evidence states that during physical activation, burn-off gases such as CO, CO₂, H₂, or CH₄ evolve, and controlled burn-off is an important factor in porosity development [N4-R2]. Another source describes physical activation as a dual-stage process featuring carbonization in the presence of an inert gas such as N₂ or Ar, followed by activation with an oxidizing gas such as O₂, CO₂, or H₂O steam, in the temperature range of 800–1200 °C [N6-F2]. This makes the atmosphere conditions highly deliberate: inert gas for carbonization and oxidizing gas for activation.

The temperature and time profiles for physical activation are more extreme than those for chemical activation. The review source explicitly states that physical activation is performed at higher temperatures, typically 800–1200 °C [N6-F2]. It also notes that physical activation can involve relatively long processing times, low carbon yield, and poor specific surface area when compared to chemical activation [N6-F2]. The evidence further indicates that the main factors affecting physical activation include the type of carbon precursors, particle size, gas flow, heating rate, carbonization time, and carbonization temperature [N6-F2]. In other words, the procedure is sensitive to both thermal and kinetic conditions during the activation step.

Before activation, the precursor is typically first carbonized. The review source says physical activation is a dual-stage process with a carbonization stage in the presence of an inert gas followed by activation under an oxidizing gas atmosphere [N6-F2]. This means the precursor is not activated directly from raw form but is first pyrolyzed and carbonized before the actual activation step begins. The evidence also suggests that the precursor chemistry matters, because the carbonization stage is part of the preparation method that shapes the final pore structure [N6-F1].

In short, physical activation is a gas-driven, two-stage process using inert and oxidizing atmospheres at higher temperatures, with the precursor first carbonized before activation [N4-R2][N6-F2]. This contrasts with chemical activation, which uses chemical reagents and operates at lower temperatures in a single stage [N3-R1][N6-F2].
node_outputs.N11:
Branch report on advantages and tradeoffs of each method

The main tradeoff between chemical and physical activation centers on temperature, control, and process complexity. Chemical activation is noted for lower heating temperatures, shorter processing time, higher carbon yield, well-controlled porosity, and higher specific surface area [N3-R1][N6-F2]. In contrast, physical activation is described as having higher activation temperatures, longer processing times, relatively low carbon yield, and poor specific surface area, especially compared to chemical activation [N6-F2]. The evidence also states that chemical activation is more advantageous in terms of lower energy cost and higher product yield, while physical activation is considered cleaner and greener, with availability of activating agents and ease of technology [N3-R3][N6-F2].

On pore size and surface area control, chemical activation appears better suited for precise control. The review source explicitly says chemical activation is advantageous for well-controlled porosity and high specific surface area [N6-F2]. It also states that chemical activation can develop micropores and mesopores, with specific activators such as ZnCl₂, H₃PO₄, and KOH significantly influencing porosity development in lignocellulosic-derived carbons [N3-R5]. This suggests that chemical activation is more easily tuned to target desired pore structures. Physical activation, by contrast, is described as being more dependent on burn-off gases and controlled burn-off, but the evidence here is less explicit about whether it is better or worse for pore-size control [N4-R2]. Still, the higher temperature range and single-stage nature of chemical activation make it more favorable for controlling porosity and surface area.

Regarding porosity and uniform structure, chemical activation is again advantaged. The review source says chemical activation is considered the most promising method for producing activated carbon with excellent performance because it can yield high specific surface area and well-controlled textural properties [N6-F2]. The evidence also mentions that chemical activation can produce materials with high microporous and mesoporous volumes [N1-R1]. Physical activation, by contrast, is associated with relatively long processing times and lower carbon yield, which may make it less uniform in some cases, though the evidence here is not as strong on uniformity as on temperature and yield [N6-F2]. Overall, chemical activation appears better at producing higher porosity and more uniform structure where precise control is needed.

For scalability and sensitivity to impurities, physical activation is described as cleaner, green, and easier in terms of technology, with availability of activating agents [N3-R3][N6-F2]. However, the same source notes that physical activation has high activation temperature and long processing time, which may make it less favorable for some scale-up contexts [N6-F2]. Chemical activation, on the other hand, is more corrosive and often requires a washing step, which can complicate downstream processing and make it more sensitive to impurities [N6-F2]. The evidence therefore suggests that physical activation may be easier to scale or less sensitive to impurities in some respects, but chemical activation is more controllable and better suited for high-performance materials.

Overall, the two methods have complementary strengths: chemical activation excels at pore-size control, surface area, and high-performance materials, while physical activation is cleaner, simpler, and more energy-efficient in some contexts [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-F2].

Branch report on synthesis context and material performance

Activation method interacts strongly with precursor chemistry. The evidence shows that precursor chemistry determines how mesoporous carbon is formed, with carbon sources such as sucrose, phenolic resin, and other precursors reacting with metal precursors or being impregnated with activators before thermal treatment [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The review source further emphasizes that the preparation method directly influences pore structure, specific surface area, pore volume, and surface chemistry, which in turn determines performance [N6-F1]. This means that the choice of precursor and its chemical treatment before activation is central to the final material properties.

Activation affects functionalization or surface chemistry by altering the surface structure and pore architecture. The review source notes that activation can improve specific surface area or pore volume and can vary or adjust the surface chemical nature of activated carbon [N6-F2]. It also states that activating agents play decisive roles in the formation of pores or surface chemical groups during activation [N6-F2]. Chemical activation, in particular, is described as involving degradation, dehydration, and complexation mechanisms that develop porosity while protecting the internal pore structure [N1-R4][N1-R2]. This indicates that activation is not merely a physical etching process but also a surface chemistry modifier.

In terms of applications, the evidence suggests that chemical activation is better suited for materials where high surface area, well-controlled porosity, and high-performance properties are important. The review source says mesoporous carbon has great potential in energy storage, catalysis, and adsorption separation because of its unique pore size distribution, high specific surface area, and excellent stability [N6-F1]. Chemical activation is especially relevant for applications requiring precise pore control, such as adsorption, catalysis, and energy storage [N6-F1][N6-F2]. Physical activation, by contrast, is described as cleaner and green, and is therefore more attractive for simpler or environmentally friendly processes [N3-R3][N6-F2]. However, the same source notes that physical activation can produce materials with lower carbon yield and relatively poor specific surface area, which may limit its suitability for applications requiring high porosity [N6-F2].

Overall, activation method and precursor chemistry are tightly coupled. Precursor chemistry shapes the starting material, while activation controls surface chemistry, pore structure, and performance [N2-R1][N6-F1]. Chemical activation is generally better for high-performance materials and precise pore control, while physical activation is often easier to implement and more environmentally favorable [N3-R3][N6-F2].
node_outputs.N10:
Branch report on pore-size control and structural mechanisms

The evidence suggests that chemical activation is generally better at creating mesopores, while physical activation is more commonly associated with micropores and can be adjusted to mesopores under certain conditions. The review source states that chemical activation can produce materials with high microporous and mesoporous volumes and that chemical activators such as ZnCl₂, H₃PO₄, and KOH significantly influence porosity development in lignocellulosic-derived carbons [N1-R1][N3-R5]. Another review source notes that chemical activation is advantageous for well-controlled porosity and high specific surface area, supporting the view that it is more tunable for pore structure [N6-F2]. In contrast, physical activation is described as a dual-stage process that can produce activated carbon with a wide pore-size distribution, but the evidence here is less explicit about whether it is inherently better for mesopores [N6-F2]. Still, the evidence does indicate that physical activation can be used to adjust pore size, as the controlled burn-off of gases is an important factor in porosity development [N4-R2].

Activation affects pore size distribution and surface area in a predictable way. Chemical activation tends to increase BET surface area, microporous volume, and mesoporous volume [N1-R1]. ## Integrated final answer comparing chemical and physical activation methods

Mesoporous carbon is prepared by activating a carbon precursor, and the choice between chemical and physical activation determines the procedural route, the pore structure, and the material’s properties. The branch reports show that these two methods differ fundamentally in how porosity is developed: **chemical activation uses chemical reagents to control porosity**, while **physical activation uses controlled burn-off gases and thermal treatment** [N8][N9].

### 1) Main procedural differences

#### Chemical activation
Chemical activation is reagent-driven. The evidence identifies specific activators such as **H₃PO₄**, **KOH**, and **ZnCl₂** as common agents used to promote bond cleavage and protect internal pore structure [N1-R2][N3-R5]. In the context of mesoporous carbon, the precursor is impregnated with a chemical agent before thermal treatment, and the process is described as the thermal decomposition of a carbon precursor impregnated with suitable chemical agents [N2-R4]. This means the precursor is not left raw; it is chemically modified before activation [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Thermally, chemical activation is carried out at lower temperatures than physical activation. One review source says chemical activation occurs in the range of **450–850 °C**, while physical activation is a dual-stage process in the range of **800–1200 °C** [N6-F2]. Another source explicitly states that chemical activation is advantageous because it operates at lower temperatures than physical activation [N3-R1]. The evidence also notes that chemical activation is a **single-stage** process in which carbonization and activation occur simultaneously, whereas physical activation is more conventionally split into carbonization followed by activation [N6-F2].

#### Physical activation
Physical activation relies on **controlled burn-off gases** such as **CO**, **CO₂**, **H₂**, or **CH₄**, and the atmosphere conditions are deliberately set to influence porosity [N4-R2][N6-F2]. The review source describes physical activation as a **dual-stage** process: first carbonization in the presence of an inert gas such as **N₂** or **Ar**, then activation with an oxidizing gas such as **O₂**, **CO₂**, or **H₂O steam** [N6-F2]. This makes physical activation a gas- and temperature-dependent process rather than a chemical-reagent-dependent one [N9].

Before activation, the precursor is typically first **carbonized**. The review source says physical activation is a dual-stage process with a carbonization stage in the presence of an inert gas followed by activation under an oxidizing gas atmosphere [N6-F2]. This means the precursor is not activated directly from raw form but is first pyrolyzed and carbonized before the actual activation step begins [N6-F1].

### 2) Which activation method better controls pore size and surface area?

The evidence strongly favors **chemical activation** for better pore-size control and surface-area control. The review source says chemical activation is advantageous for **well-controlled porosity** and **high specific surface area** [N6-F2]. Physical activation is less clearly described as being better for pore-size control. Still, the review source notes that physical activation can produce activated carbon with a wide pore-size distribution [N6-F2]. So, while physical activation can be used to develop pores, the evidence suggests it is less precise than chemical activation for fine control.

Chemical activation appears better at producing **higher porosity** and **more uniform structure** where precise control is needed. Physical activation is less favorable for high porosity in the evidence provided. The review source notes that physical activation can have **relatively low carbon yield** and **poor specific surface area**, especially compared to chemical activation [N6-F2]. It also notes that physical activation is conventionally split into a **dual-stage** process, which may make the resulting structure less uniform or more sensitive to process conditions [N6-F2]. Chemical activation is best suited for applications where **high surface area**, **well-controlled porosity**, and **high-performance properties** are important. Chemical activation is therefore especially relevant for applications such as **adsorption**, **catalytic support**, and **energy storage** [N6-F1][N6-F2].

Physical activation is more attractive for simpler or environmentally favorable processes. It is described as **cleaner**, **green**, and easier in terms of technology [N3-R3][N6-F2]. Still, physical activation remains a viable method when the goal is to produce activated carbon with a **wide pore-size distribution** or when environmental or technological simplicity is a priority [N6-F2].

### Bottom line

The main procedural difference is that **chemical activation uses chemical reagents** to control porosity, while **physical activation uses controlled burn-off gases** and thermal treatment [N8][N9].
